finding.title: Horizontal
finding.rationale: In vuln=1 branch (books.py:50), the query is Book.query.filter_by(book_title=str(book_title)).first() with NO ownership filter. The JWT sub is validated (token_validator line 46) but never used to restrict which book is returned.
finding.evidence: exploitable=True | role=Any authenticated user (role: user) | side_effect=Any authenticated user reads the secret_content of any other user's book by supplying its title in the path parameter | witness=Register/login as argus_test, then GET /books/v1/bookTitle77 (owned by name1) — response returns secret_content without any ownership validation | notes=Confirmed live in recon. The book title acts as the sole access key; GET /books/v1 (public) reveals all titles and their owners, making enumeration trivial.

finding.title: Horizontal
finding.rationale: In vuln=1 branch (users.py:186), the target user is resolved via User.query.filter_by(username=username).first() where username is the PATH PARAM. JWT sub is validated (token_validator line 181) but the identity from resp['sub'] is never compared to the path param username — no ownership binding.
finding.evidence: exploitable=True | role=Any authenticated user (role: user) | side_effect=Any authenticated user resets any other user's password to an arbitrary value, enabling full account takeover | witness=Login as argus_test, then PUT /users/v1/name1/password with body {"password": "hacked"} — name1's password is changed without ownership validation | notes=Confirmed live in recon. The secure branch (vuln=0, users.py:194) correctly uses resp['sub'] as the target. This is BFLA — a function-level authorization failure combined with IDOR.

finding.title: Authentication_Bypass
finding.rationale: Authentication requirement (Bearer token check) on the debug endpoint. Endpoint should be removed entirely from production code or gated by the vuln flag at minimum. Currently not gated by any auth check and not controlled by the vulnerable environment variable.
finding.evidence: exploitable=True | notes=Live-confirmed: unauthenticated GET /users/v1/_debug returns HTTP 200 with full credential dump including admin:pass1 with admin=true. This endpoint is unconditionally present in both vulnerable=0 and vulnerable=1 modes — it is NOT gated by the vuln flag. This is the most direct complete authentication bypass: no cracking, no exploitation, just a single GET request.

finding.title: Login_Flow_Logic
finding.rationale: Server-side role assignment only (never accept role from client input); additionalProperties: false in register_user_schema to reject extra fields including 'admin'.
finding.evidence: exploitable=True | notes=Live-confirmed: registered test_mass_assign_xyz with admin:true; /users/v1/_debug confirmed admin=True on new account. JSON schema register_user_schema only requires username/password/email — no additionalProperties restriction. Vuln flag controls this branch (vuln=1 deployed).

finding.title: Transport_Exposure
finding.rationale: Cache-Control: no-store and Pragma: no-cache response headers on all authentication responses containing tokens or credentials.
finding.evidence: exploitable=True | notes=Live-confirmed: no Cache-Control or Pragma headers in any response. JWT returned in response body (not Set-Cookie) makes it more likely to be cached by intermediate layers. Lower exploitability than AUTH-VULN-01/02 since caching of POST responses is non-default, but absence of cache headers is a confirmed gap.

finding.title: SQLi
finding.data_flow: source=username path parameter; api_views/users.py:45 (Connexion routes GET /users/v1/{username} to get_by_username) | sink=models/user_model.py:73 — db.session.execute(text(user_query)) | path=get_by_username (api_views/users.py:45) → User.get_user(username) (models/user_model.py:70) → f-string SQL construction (models/user_model.py:72) → db.session.execute(text(user_query)) (models/user_model.py:73)
finding.rationale: The username path parameter is directly interpolated into a raw SQL string via Python f-string at models/user_model.py:72 with zero sanitization. SQLAlchemy's text() wrapper does NOT provide parameterization — it merely marks the string as safe to execute as raw SQL. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL clauses (UNION, subqueries, comments) to manipulate query structure.
finding.evidence: exploitable=True | verdict=vulnerable | witness=' UNION SELECT 1,username,3,password,5 FROM users-- | notes=Unauthenticated endpoint — no Bearer token required. SQLite backend: UNION SELECT, sqlite_master, and LIMIT/OFFSET are all supported. Response reflects injected query output: ret[1] appears as 'username' field, ret[3] as 'email' field in the JSON response (models/user_model.py:76). get_user() is called TWICE per request (api_views/users.py:46 and 47), executing the injected SQL twice. The UNION payload targets the password column in the email slot to exfiltrate credentials. vuln flag must be 1 (confirmed at runtime via app.py:9).

finding.title: IDOR in get book by title (vulnerable path)
finding.data_flow: HTTP request with book_title -> get_by_title -> token_validator (authenticated) -> if vuln: Book.query.filter_by(book_title=...) without owner filter -> returns secret content
finding.rationale: After passing the authentication token check, the vulnerable branch (if vuln:) ignores the ownership relationship and retrieves any book by title. This allows an authenticated user to read another user’s secret content—a classic IDOR.
finding.remediation: Always scope the book query to the authenticated user (e.g., Book.query.filter_by(user=current_user, book_title=...)). Remove the vulnerable branch or protect it with the same ownership check.

finding.title: Horizontal password change for arbitrary user (vulnerable path)
finding.data_flow: HTTP request with username and new password -> update_password -> token_validator -> if vuln: User.query.filter_by(username=username).first() (no owner check) -> updates password of any user
finding.rationale: After passing the token check, the vulnerable branch uses the URL parameter username to fetch the target user, ignoring the token’s subject. This allows any authenticated user to change another user’s password.
finding.evidence:
Source excerpt:
    if vuln:
        user = User.query.filter_by(username=username).first()
        if user:
            user.password = request_data.get('password')
            db.session.commit()

No verification that the token’s sub matches the target username.
finding.remediation: Always update the password of the user identified by the token (resp['sub']). Remove the vulnerable code path or add an ownership check (e.g., only admin or self).

finding.title: Unauthenticated exposure of all credentials via debug endpoint
finding.data_flow: HTTP request -> debug() -> User.get_all_users_debug() -> User.json_debug() -> response includes password field
finding.rationale: The /users/debug endpoint has no authentication check and returns all users' records, including plaintext passwords and admin status. This completely breaks identity confidentiality.
finding.evidence: debug function lacks any token_validator or authorization call. json_debug method explicitly includes password and admin fields in its returned dictionary.
finding.remediation: Remove the debug endpoint entirely in production, or protect it with strong authentication and strip passwords from the response. The json_debug method must never include secrets.

finding.title: Privilege escalation via unauthenticated admin creation
finding.data_flow: HTTP POST /register with {"admin": true} -> register_user -> if vuln and 'admin' in request_data: admin = True -> creates admin user without any auth
finding.rationale: The registration endpoint is public and uses a flag (vuln) to allow the caller to set the admin role. No authentication or role check is performed, enabling anyone to instantly gain administrative access.
finding.remediation: Never trust incoming role attributes. Set admin=False on every self-registration, or require an existing authenticated admin to create privileged accounts.

finding.title: Passwords stored in plaintext
finding.data_flow: User creation (User.__init__) stores password as-is -> login_user compares request password with user.password directly
finding.rationale: The application stores and compares passwords in plaintext. If the database is compromised, all credentials are immediately exposed. This violates basic password storage security requirements.
finding.evidence: User::__init__ assigns 'self.password = password'. login_user performs 'request_data.get('password') == user.password' with no hashing.
finding.remediation: Hash passwords using a strong, salted, one-way algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2. Store only the hash. During login, hash the supplied password and compare with the stored hash.

finding.title: SQL Injection in User.get_user
finding.data_flow: username parameter -> get_by_username -> User.get_user (raw SQL f-string) -> db.session.execute
finding.rationale: The username from the URL is directly interpolated into an SQL query string without parameterization, allowing an attacker to modify the query structure.
finding.evidence: In models/user_model.py:72, user_query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}'" and then executed via db.session.execute(text(user_query)).
finding.remediation: Use parameterized query: db.session.execute(text('SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = :username'), {'username': username}) or rely on ORM methods like User.query.filter_by(username=username).first().

unadjudicated_findings.title: Missing authentication on user information endpoint
User enumeration via login error messages
Unauthenticated access to all books list
Unauthenticated debug disclosure of all user credentials
